# Lichii Lichii is an experimental, open-source Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 emulator written in C++. It builds on Eglantine, Eden, yuzu and Sudachi, preserving their contributions while developing this fork's game compatibility and renderer fixes. This is an independent fork, not an official release of those upstream projects. Lichii is not affiliated with Nintendo. Visit the [Lichii game compatibility website](https://lichii.zortos.me) to find games and compare community compatibility reports. ## Downloads and setup Download Lichii only from this repository's [releases page](https://github.com/zortos293/Lichii/releases). Lichii has no other download site: archives offered elsewhere, such as lichii.org, are not built by this project, and one has been reported to install malware ([#545](https://github.com/zortos293/Lichii/issues/545)). On Windows, extract the entire build archive and run **lichii.exe**. Only use games and system files you have legally obtained. Games, keys and firmware are not included. ### Existing saves and settings Lichii uses its own profile: `%APPDATA%\lichii` on Windows, and the `lichii` directories under `$XDG_DATA_HOME`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` on Linux and macOS. Without XDG overrides, these are `~/.local/share/lichii`, `~/.config/lichii` and `~/.cache/lichii`. An existing portable `user/` directory still takes priority and is not imported or changed by the wizard. On the first non-portable GUI launch, Lichii offers to import Eden and other detected emulator profiles. Back up `%APPDATA%\eden` first on Windows, or the old data, config and cache directories on Unix, and close the source emulator. Choose **Keep Old Data** to copy without changing the source, then check your saves and relaunch. Existing destination data is retained in backup directories rather than merged. Move also retains a source backup until you remove it yourself; Link deliberately shares settings and saves. Paths outside the imported data root remain shared and unchanged. An interrupted import offers recovery on the next launch. `eden-cli`, including `--help` and `--version`, refuses to initialize configuration until you import or explicitly choose **Start fresh** in the GUI. ## Compatibility and issue reports Compatibility and performance vary by game, hardware and driver. Rendering errors, stutters and crashes remain possible. Passing automated tests does not establish that a game renders correctly, and this project makes no universal frame-rate guarantee. Browse [community compatibility reports](https://lichii.zortos.me/reports) for results with each player's build and setup. Desktop reporting requires a build containing [PR #303](https://github.com/zortos293/Lichii/pull/303) and is not available in build 88. In builds that include it, play and stop a Switch 2 game, then right-click that game and choose **Submit compatibility report**. Only the latest session in the current Lichii process is eligible. Confirm the matching website catalog entry and review the editable machine, game, setup, and enabled add-on details prefilled where available. Check the public preview and give explicit consent before submitting. Nothing uploads automatically, and the native v1 reporter does not read or upload logs or files. When [reporting an issue](https://github.com/zortos293/Eglantine/issues), include: - The exact build, game version, CPU, GPU and driver version. - Relevant settings and steps to reproduce the problem. - A screenshot and the log from the affected session, after checking it for personal information. Do not upload game files, keys, firmware or private account information. ## Building and contributing See the [build guide](docs/Build.md), [user documentation](docs/user/README.md) and [coding guidelines](docs/Coding.md). To uninstall, run `uninstall.cmd` or `sh uninstall.sh` with the same folder. ## Supported GPUs - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 20, 30, 40 and 50 series, and GTX 16 series - AMD Radeon RX 5000, 6000, 7000 and 9000 series, and Steam Deck - Intel Arc A and B series On Windows 10 and 11, and on Linux and SteamOS with Proton. ## Results and problems Please post them as [issues](../../issues/new/choose): - **Performance results**: run the test kit from the release and attach its result file. - **Problems**: the game, GPU and driver, operating system, settings and what you saw, with the newest `nr_fg-*.log` from under the game's `OptiScaler/custom/Apex Neural Rendering FG` folder. OptiScaler is GPL-3.0; its source for each release is attached to the release. ## Record and compare frame generation nr-record records the inputs a game gives its frame generation, losslessly. You can then replay a recording through any frame generation DLL you have (ANR FG, a game's DLSS-G `nvngx_dlssg.dll`) and compare the results as videos or images. nr-record includes no frame generation. Requirements: - a D3D12 or Vulkan game with DLSS frame generation, with the `anr-fg-full` package installed (it includes OptiScaler); - Windows 10 or 11, or Linux with Proton; - [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html) and ffprobe on the `PATH`; - for DLSS-G replays, an NVIDIA RTX 40 or 50 series GPU. 1. **Install.** Download `nr-record-1.2-windows.zip` or `nr-record-1.2-linux.tar.gz` from the [FG-V.B18 release](../../releases/tag/FG-V.B18) and extract it. Close the game and run the installer with the folder of the game's `.exe`: - Windows: `install.cmd ""`. No launch option is needed. - Linux and Steam Deck (Proton): `sh install.sh ""`. Set the game's Steam launch options to `WINEDLLOVERRIDES="dxgi=n,b" %command%` (the ANR FG installer prints the same line). Do not set this on Windows: the game may not start. The installer copies `nr-record` into `OptiScaler/custom/` and sets `FGNvngxReplacement=nr-record` in `OptiScaler.ini` (it keeps the original). When you are not recording, ANR FG generates the frames, or DLSS-G if ANR FG is not installed (`forward` in `nr-record/dlssg/nr_record.ini`). `uninstall.cmd` or `sh uninstall.sh` with the same folder removes nr-record and restores `OptiScaler.ini`. Website  ·  Blog  ·  Slack  ·  Apache-2.0

macOS / Metal  ·  Linux / CUDA  ·  Windows (in progress)

**Run models larger than your RAM or VRAM.** InferSSD builds on [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) to run large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models from SSD, using standard GGUF files, with browser chat and an OpenAI-compatible API. It supports **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017**, **Muse-Spark-Open**, **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B** and **Qwen3.8 Flash Next**, plus ordinary RAM inference for **Gemma4 E4B**. ## Models These are the tested GGUF files, community conversions of the named model releases. DeepSeek's Q8_0 keeps the official bit widths: routed experts stay native 4-bit MXFP4, and FP8 tensors become 8-bit Q8_0. See [weight-format details](docs/benchmark.md#checkpoint-formats). | Model | Parameter count | GGUF reference | | --- | --- | --- | | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | 763B total / 8–16B active | [mrfakename · Q8_0](https://huggingface.co/mrfakename/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-GGUF) | | Muse-Spark-Open | 816B total / 42B active | [Unsloth · UD-Q4_K_XL](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF) | | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 35B total / 3B active | [Unsloth · UD-Q4_K_XL](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF) | | Qwen3.8 Flash Next | 177B total / A3B | [Bartowski · IQ4_XS](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) | | Gemma4 E4B | 7.46B total / E4B | [Google · QAT Q4_0](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf) | Gemma uses the ordinary native loader without SSD expert offload. Before loading, the shared launcher checks that weights, KV cache and working memory fit the memory budget, the machine's physical memory unless a smaller one is configured; the system pages other memory out to make room. On Apple silicon the per-layer embedding table, 2.15 GiB of the 4.80 GiB file, stays in the file and its rows are read from the SSD as tokens use them; the other weights are held in memory. A model that does not fit is rejected. macOS and Windows use the same model selection and launch entry points. ## Performance benchmarks **4K prompt tier · 256 output tokens · decode measured over tokens 129–256.** All rates are in **token/s**; higher is faster. The multiple next to each **InferSSD** rate is its speedup over llama.cpp on the same hardware. On the MacBook Pro, Colibri runs the official Safetensors on CPU; llama.cpp and InferSSD run the GGUF with Metal. content.readme:
# GTA: Vice City Stories — Native PC port (PS2 static recompilation)

A native **Windows and Linux** port of **Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories** (PS2, USA, SLUS-21590), made by
recompiling the game's PS2 executable into C++. Both are built from the same source and run natively: Direct3D 11 on
Windows, Vulkan on Linux.

**This repository contains no game code or game data.** You need your own copy of the game as an `.iso`.
The build reads the executable from your disc, and the finished game reads everything else from it while it runs.

Status: in development. See [docs/PROGRESS.md](docs/PROGRESS.md) for what works, and [docs/LINUX.md](docs/LINUX.md)
for the Linux build in detail.

## Install on Windows: the launcher (easiest)

1. Download the newest `VCS-Recomp-<version>-windows.zip` from the [Releases](../../releases) page and extract it
   somewhere short and local, like `C:\Games\VCS` (not Program Files, not a OneDrive-synced folder such as Desktop or
   Documents: the build writes thousands of files).
2. Start **`VCSLauncher.exe`** in that folder. It walks you through four steps, one at a time, then shows a big
   **Play** button:
   - **Folder**: the game is built in `build\` next to the launcher, or in a folder you choose (another drive with
     more room, say): *Choose another folder* on this step.
   - **Disc**: it looks for your `.iso` in Downloads, Desktop, Documents and its own folder; otherwise choose it (or
     drag it onto the window, or copy your disc from a DVD drive). It checks that it is the USA release.
   - **Build tools**: the game is compiled on your PC with Microsoft's free C++ tools. If they are missing,
     *Install build tools* runs Microsoft's installer with the right options (about 6 GB; Windows asks for permission).
   - **Build**: recompiles the game from your disc and compiles it, with a progress bar - 20 to 60 minutes the first
     time, a few minutes after an update. Nothing is downloaded during the build: the release brings Python and the
     libraries.
   - **Play**.

The launcher also backs up and restores your saves, makes a desktop shortcut, checks for a new release (only when you
ask, or at start if you turn that on in *Settings*), and zips the logs into a report for bug reports. Windows may warn
that the launcher is from an unknown publisher (it isn't signed): *More info > Run anyway*. How it works:
[docs/LAUNCHER.md](docs/LAUNCHER.md). Everything it does is a script in `tools/` you can also run yourself (below).
If the *Pricedown* font (GTA's lettering, free for personal desktop use from Typodermic) is installed on your PC, the
launcher uses it for its title and Play button; its licence doesn't allow including it, so it isn't.

## Install on Linux: the launcher (easiest)

1. Download the newest `VCS-Recomp-<version>-x86_64.AppImage` from the [Releases](../../releases) page. It runs on
   any 64-bit desktop with glibc 2.35 or newer: Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Linux Mint 21, Fedora, Arch and later, on
   X11 or Wayland. It needs a Vulkan driver (Mesa or NVIDIA's) and `python3`, which every desktop has.
2. Make it executable and start it: in the file manager, *Properties > Permissions > Allow executing as a program*, or
   `chmod +x VCS-Recomp-*.AppImage && ./VCS-Recomp-*.AppImage`. The first start puts the game's files (the source,
   the scripts, the libraries) in `~/.local/share/VCSRecomp/install`, where the game is built, then walks you through
   the same steps as on Windows:
   - **Folder**: where the game is built (another drive with more room: *Choose another folder*).
   - **Disc**: your `.iso` from Downloads, Desktop or Documents, chosen, or dropped onto the window.
   - **Build tools**: the compiler (clang 19 or newer) and the libraries the build needs, from your distribution.
     *Install packages* asks for your password and installs them; *Install in a terminal* shows the command instead.
     On Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12, whose clang is older, it adds LLVM's own repository ([apt.llvm.org](https://apt.llvm.org)) first.

The decompilation of FNV, the Steam release for PC (version 1.4.0.525): C++ source code rebuilt function by function
from the game's executable. Built with the compilers the game was built with, every function listed in
`build/units.json` compiles to the same bytes as the original.

The project was spearheaded on [fnvdecomp.com](https://fnvdecomp.com), where a frozen version of the community
project stays online.

- **What it is for.** The modding community has kept working on FNV for more than a decade. This repository is meant
  for that community: for research, modding and game preservation, and only those purposes.
- **Source code only.** It contains no game files, no assets, no executables and nothing you can play, and nothing
  of the game is distributed here.
- **You need the game.** To use any of this you need to own the Steam version of FNV (1.4.0.525).

Pull requests are welcome from anyone. Most of what is left is readability: many functions still have placeholder
names (`FUN_00xxxxxx`), vague names or no comment, and all of that can be improved without changing a single byte of
the output.

### The automatic check

Every pull request gets an automatic check, called `match`. It runs on GitHub's machines, involves no part of the
game, and has to pass before a pull request can be merged:

1. It finds the translation units your change can affect: the files you changed, every unit that includes them, and
   every unit whose entry in `build/units.json` changed.
2. It builds each of those units twice, from `main` and with your change, with the Microsoft compilers the game was
   built with.
3. Every function has to come out identical, at its original address: the same code bytes, and every call and data
   reference resolving to the same original address through `build/units.json`, exception-handling code included.
   A function that moved to another unit is compared with what it compiled to in its old unit. `main` matches the
   game byte for byte, so a change that passes still does.

What to expect:

- **Passes:** renaming functions, parameters, variables, types and fields; adding or improving comments;
  reformatting; restructuring headers and types; moving functions between units (see "Changing the build recipe"). A
  change only to comments, spacing or blank lines passes without a build.
- **Fails:** anything that changes what a function compiles to. The check lists the functions that differ by
  address; see what differs with your own copy of the game:
  `python3 tools/build_and_match.py --image <your FalloutNV.exe> --only <unit>`.
- **Needs a maintainer:** changes outside `src/`, `include/`, `build/units.json` and Markdown files (the tools, the
  workflow), and changes to `build/units.json` beyond what "Changing the build recipe" allows. The check fails on
  these and nobody can merge them, so open an issue instead. Changes to the tools and the workflow are made by the
  repository owner and verified against the game.

### Review and merging

A pull request is merged when the check passes and two reviewers have approved it:

- Nobody can skip the check, the repository owner included.
- Two approvals are needed. An approval is dropped when new commits arrive, and the last push has to be approved by
  someone other than the person who made it.
- The pull request has to be up to date with `main`. If `main` moves first, use "Update branch" and the check runs
  again on the combined code.

After every change to `main`, the whole of `main` is also built against the game's executable on the project's own
machine. That build proves `main` still matches the game byte for byte, not only that it compiles the same as
before.

### Renaming a function

`build/units.json` lists every function by its original address and its decorated (mangled) name. When you rename a
function, put its new decorated name at the same address, in every unit that lists it; otherwise the check reports
the old name as unbound. Adding a declaration or a string literal can renumber the compiler's string labels
(`$SG...`) that `build/units.json` names; the check says so when that is the cause.

A unit may also bind a name to an address it refers to, for example a global or a vtable that the code used to write
as a number: the check builds the unit again and the bytes at every function's address have to stay the same.
Exception-handling code resolves names through the whole of `build/units.json`, so when a pull request changes any

content.readme:
Kernarium
===

Run a real Linux kernel natively on iOS, through the magic of [User-mode Linux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-mode_Linux).

## Apps

### Andarium

An Android emulator app built on the Kernarium runtime is available in [TestFlight beta](https://testflight.apple.com/join/qyPvJTUE). Source code is available under [`Andarium/`](/Andarium/).

The TestFlight beta only has 10,000 tester slots and gets filled up quickly. Alternatively, you can sideload IPA from [releases](https://github.com/imxieyi/Kernarium/releases).

### Kernarium

A generic Linux emulator app capable of running various Linux distributions. It's still at an early stage of development and isn't ready for release yet. Source code is available under [`Kernarium/`](/Kernarium/).

## Overview

The User-mode Linux kernel is compiled to native arm64 code, then linked to an iOS runtime framework. The kernel runs natively without emulation. Userspace programs are emulated using an [iSH](https://github.com/ish-app/ish)-style threaded interpreter, with SMP support. Guest GPU acceleration is provided by [KosmicKrisp](https://docs.mesa3d.org/drivers/kosmickrisp.html), a translation layer from Vulkan to Metal.

This emulator architecture sits between a full system emulator (like [UTM](https://github.com/utmapp/UTM)) and a full userspace emulator (like [iSH](https://github.com/ish-app/ish)). It combines the benefits of a real Linux kernel and a userspace emulator that only needs to emulate userspace code. It's capable of running advanced workloads including Docker containers, Linux desktops, Wine/Proton and a full Android system at decent speed on modern iOS devices.

## Features

- Kernel
    - Mainline 6.18 LTS kernel for both Linux and Android guests
    - Supports most kernel features, including namespaces, SELinux and more
- CPU emulation
    - Supports `arm64`, `arm32`, `x86_64` guest instructions
    - Both interpreter and JIT execution modes (interpreter-only for TestFlight release)
- GPU acceleration
    - Vulkan 1.4 via [KosmicKrisp](https://docs.mesa3d.org/drivers/kosmickrisp.html)
    - OpenGL 4.6 & GLES 3.2 via [Zink](https://docs.mesa3d.org/drivers/zink.html)
    - Hardware video encoding and decoding (H.264, HEVC) via [VideoToolbox](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/videotoolbox)
- Storage
    - Supports virtual disks via UBD driver, with discard support
    - Supports any Linux filesystem including ext2/3/4, erofs, xfs, ...
    - Supports loop devices and FUSE
- Network
    - Full Linux networking stack
    - Guest network access via [libslirp](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/slirp/libslirp)

## Build or Embed

Point your coding agent at this repo if you want to build the project or embed its runtime in other apps. The agent guide is [`AGENTS.md`](/AGENTS.md), and the documentation is under [`docs/`](/docs/).

Building Android system image requires a powerful remote x86_64 Linux building machine ([requirements](https://source.android.com/docs/setup/start/requirements)). Alternatively, you can download prebuilt images from [releases](https://github.com/imxieyi/Kernarium/releases) and point your coding agent at it.
